claims.text: This is a soba (buckwheat) shop whose noodles are blended with sarashina flour and roasted-tea powder; wheat is standard in soba dough and in the dipping sauce. No gluten-free handling is documented.
Soba is served with a traditional soy-sauce-and-dashi tsuyu, which is normally wheat-based; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Traditional soba tsuyu is based on katsuobushi/animal dashi; no vegan dashi or menu is documented.
The official site and menu publish no formal allergen or cross-contamination protocol; the cafe lists a direct phone line (076-255-0370) for dietary questions.
All pancakes are made from 100% Ishikawa-grown Koshihikari rice flour with no wheat — the entire pancake concept is gluten-free, making this a genuine GF destination.
The batter contains only rice flour, meringue (egg whites), milk, and a little salt, so the core product avoids wheat thickeners entirely.

name: Cajon to Seed（カホントゥシード） (Cajon to Seed)

claims.text: Published menus describe additive-free seasonings (including soy-sauce-style products from a traditional Ishikawa maker) and Asian/Thai preparations, so wheat-containing sauces are likely present; no gluten-free assurance is documented.

The omnivore kitchen plates seafood (shrimp, tuna), chicken and egg components alongside vegetable dishes on the same changing lunch set, so plant-only diners should confirm which items are free of animal products that week.
Strong base of plant-based items — organic salad, pesticide-free brown rice, vegetable soup, smoothies and fresh juices — gives vegetarians and vegans workable options.
Ingredients are emphasized as organic, pesticide-free and additive-free, including brown rice from the restaurant's own paddies.
All oden items simmer together in a single shared fish-and-soy dashi pot, so even non-wheat items share the broth.
The broth is seasoned with local soy sauce, which standardly contains wheat; house-made fish cakes (chikuwa, hanpen, fritters) are also typically wheat-bound surimi.
The base dashi is made from bonito and dried fish, so all simmered items — including vegetables — are cooked in animal stock.
Dashi and fish cakes are made fresh in house daily, so staff know exactly what goes into each item and can be asked about ingredients in person.
A wheat-flour bakery where bread is the entire product line, so airborne flour and shared surfaces make cross-contamination unavoidable; not celiac-safe.
Dairy- and egg-rich items (lemon cake, scones, cookies) are made in the same small kitchen as the breads, so shared equipment is likely; no vegan separation is documented.

name: 第7ギョーザの店 (Dai-7 Gyoza no Mise)

claims.text: Gyoza are fried/cooked in shared oil and equipment; the entire core menu is wheat-flour dumplings, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.
Standard gyoza dipping sauce (soy sauce / vinegar / chili oil) is used; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
Dumplings are pork-based and cooked on shared meat equipment; no vegan options documented.
As a traditional sushi counter, soy sauce (typically brewed with wheat) is used throughout; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The menu is built entirely around fish and shellfish (nodoguro, white shrimp, anago); broths and rice seasoning likely include fish-based ingredients.

The shop's entire concept is namafu — fresh wheat gluten — so wheat is the core ingredient throughout. There is no gluten-free path here; cross-contamination is moot because the food itself is wheat protein.
The mitarashi sauce topping is a soy-sauce-based sweet glaze, which typically contains wheat-derived soy sauce.
Several signature options are plant-based: shira-tama namafu with anko (red bean), kinako (soybean flour), or mitarashi are all dairy- and egg-free.
